newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Salomon Bros bullish on Asian equity markets.
newsitem.headline: Salomon Bros bullish on Asian equity markets.

text.p: Giant U.S. investment bank Salomon Bros on Monday painted a bullish outlook for Asian equity markets, saying share prices were falling back to earth.
The bank's Asia-Pacific co-chief executive, Trevor Rowe, said ballooning asset prices across the region had been pricked and portfolio investment funds were set to return.
"Market values are converging back to where we think the intrinsic values are, so markets are going to see a lot more portfolio investment flowing back into the region," he said.

Addressing a meeting in Melbourne organised by business think-tank, the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia, Rowe said he expected continued strong growth in Hong Kong-listed China stocks, or red chips.
He also forecast recovery for the region's depressed electronics industry, which helps drive the economies of Singapore, Korea, Malaysia and Taiwan in particular.
"We think it's turned the bottom," Rowe said.
The troubled Thai stock market is bottoming out, he added.
Thai stocks have been hit by a collapse of local property prices and a surge in bad debts. "It's either at the bottom or pretty close to the bottom," Rowe told Reuters.
Salomon Bros believes the recent slowdown in Asian economic growth, due largely to a correction in asset prices and a depressed electronics industry, is also nearing an end.
"We've seen some dramatic slowing in this last two to three-year period in the growth rates of Asian economies, but we think they are poised for another resurgence of growth," he said.

Rowe was also bullish on China, forecasting continued high levels of infrastructure investment, annual economic growth rates of around eight to 10 percent and continued emphasis on the country's private sector.
"In a macro (economic) sense, they are actually managing the economy very well," he said.
Rowe suggested more civil disturbances could be expected in Indonesia.
He said recent riots in Indonesia come against a backdrop of political transition, as the nation prepares for the eventual succession of President Suharto who has ruled for three decades.
"I am optimistic about Indonesia, but I think you are going to see a lot more disturbances as the transition takes place," he said.
